course.title: AWS Certified AI Practitioner — the Bedrock Studio
course.description: Stand up one small generative-AI assistant on Amazon Bedrock and a free local model: name the workloads, ground every answer, build a grounded app, add language and documents, weigh responsible AI, secure it and hand it over. Built for AIF-C01.
course.audience: Build, evaluate and hand over one small AI assistant as a four-person studio — everyone writes prompts, pastes the proof and fills every record; the focus decides which record you lead.

roles.name: AI Concepts (Capabilities Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the capabilities map and the responsible-AI assessment: what each workload does and its risks.

roles.name: Bedrock Build (Solution Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the build record: the invoked model, the chat app and the agent on Bedrock.

roles.name: Language & Documents (Services Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the services log: text, sentiment and the data read from a document.

roles.name: Studio Records (Governance Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the records that outlive the studio: evaluation, the risk register, custody and handover.

tasks.title: Open the accounts and guard the spend
tasks.objective: Open the AWS free account, set a $1 budget alert, and record who holds what.
definitionOfDone: The free account is open and signed into the console with MFA on
A budget of $1 alerts by email before anything can run up a bill
The register names who holds the account and who can deploy

steps.title: Open the free account and turn MFA on
steps.description: The console opens to an account the team owns, with MFA required at sign-in.
steps.instruction: Create the AWS free account for the studio and turn on multi-factor sign-in before anything else.
steps.expectedOutput: The console opens to an account the team owns, with MFA required at sign-in.
instructionList: Use a shared studio email the team agrees on, not a personal one.
Complete the free-account sign-up; on-demand Bedrock calls are kept tiny for this course.
Turn on MFA for the root user, then make an IAM user for daily work.
steps.whatItMeans: The account is the one thing a bill can grow on. MFA and a known owner are the first controls, before any model is invoked.

steps.title: Set a $1 budget alert from the shell
steps.description: Set a $1 budget alert from the shell
steps.instruction: Open CloudShell, confirm who you are, and create a $1 monthly budget that emails the studio before any spend adds up.

commands.cmd: aws sts get-caller-identity --output table
commands.explain: Confirms the account and identity you are signed in as before creating anything.

commands.cmd: aws budgets describe-budgets --account-id 123456789012 2>/dev/null || echo "no budget yet — create a $1 budget in Billing"
commands.explain: Lists budgets; create the $1 alert in Billing if none exists.
commands.sample: no budget yet — create a $1 budget in Billing

steps.whatItMeans: A budget alert is the on-demand seatbelt: the email arrives long before a forgotten job can cost real money.

outputHighlights.label: The account you are signed in to.

fixes.symptom: aws is not found in CloudShell?
fixes.fix: Open AWS CloudShell from the console top bar; the AWS CLI is built in there.

fixes.symptom: No permission to read budgets?
fixes.fix: The account owner creates the $1 budget once in Billing, then everyone can read it.

tasks.title: Run a model on your own machine
tasks.objective: Install Ollama, pull a small model, and prove it answers a prompt with no internet.
definitionOfDone: Ollama is installed and lists at least one pulled model
The model answers a prompt from the command line
The model and its size are recorded in the register

steps.title: Install Ollama and pull a small model
steps.description: Install Ollama and pull a small model
steps.instruction: Install Ollama from its official site, then pull a small model and list what you have.

commands.cmd: ollama pull llama3.2 && ollama list
commands.explain: Downloads a small model and lists the models now on disk with their sizes.
commands.sample:
NAME            ID            SIZE      MODIFIED
llama3.2:latest a80c4f17acd5  2.0 GB    5 seconds ago

steps.expectedOutput:
NAME            ID            SIZE      MODIFIED
llama3.2:latest a80c4f17acd5  2.0 GB    5 seconds ago
steps.whatItMeans: A model small enough to run on a laptop teaches the shape of every larger one, and it runs with no account and no bill.

outputHighlights.label: The model is on disk and ready to answer.

fixes.symptom: ollama is not found?
fixes.fix: Install it from the official download for your operating system, then open a new terminal.

fixes.symptom: The pull is very slow or fails?
fixes.fix: A smaller tag such as llama3.2:1b downloads faster on a thin connection.

steps.title: Prove it answers offline
steps.description: Prove it answers offline
steps.instruction: Ask the model one question from the command line and read the completion it writes back.

commands.cmd: ollama run llama3.2 "In one sentence, what is a token in a language model?"
commands.explain: Runs the model once and prints its completion to the terminal.
commands.sample: A token is a chunk of text — often a word or part of a word — that a language model reads and predicts one at a time.

steps.expectedOutput: A token is a chunk of text — often a word or part of a word — that a language model reads and predicts one at a time.
steps.whatItMeans: The prompt goes in, the completion comes out: the whole loop of a language model, on your own machine, before a single Bedrock call is made.

outputHighlights.label: The model answered the prompt locally.

tasks.title: Know your team, your focus and the folder
tasks.objective: Agree who leads which record, name the assistant, and make the studio folder every artifact goes in.
definitionOfDone: Each of the four focuses has a named member
The assistant has a name in the pattern studio-t<team>
The studio folder exists with a week-0 to week-4 layout

steps.title: Pick the focus and name the assistant
steps.description: Four names against four focuses, and an assistant name the whole team uses from now on.
steps.instruction: Agree who leads AI Concepts, Bedrock Build, Language & Documents and Studio Records. Name the assistant studio-t and your team number, and write both into the register.
steps.expectedOutput: Four names against four focuses, and an assistant name the whole team uses from now on.
steps.whatItMeans: A focus is the record a member leads and reviews, not the only work they do. Everyone writes prompts and everyone pastes output.

steps.title: Make the studio folder
steps.description: Make the studio folder
steps.instruction: Create the studio folder with a subfolder for each week. Every prompt, transcript and screenshot goes under the week it belongs to.

commands.cmd: mkdir -p studio-t1/week-{0,1,2,3,4} && ls studio-t1
commands.explain: Five week folders in one command, then reads them back. Replace t1 with your team number.

steps.expectedOutput: week-0  week-1  week-2  week-3  week-4
steps.whatItMeans: An artifact nobody can find is an artifact nobody can hash. The folder is the first custody control.

tasks.title: Name the workloads behind the features
tasks.objective: Take real product features and tag each with the AI or ML workload behind it, and what that workload can and cannot do.
definitionOfDone: Each feature is tagged with one AI or ML workload and why
Each workload has one thing it is good at and one limit
At least one feature is marked "not AI" with the reason

steps.title: Tag ten features with their workload
steps.description: Ten features, each with one workload tag and a sentence saying why it is that one.
steps.instruction: List ten features you have used, and tag each with its workload: supervised ML, unsupervised ML, computer vision, NLP or generative AI.
steps.expectedOutput: Ten features, each with one workload tag and a sentence saying why it is that one.
instructionList: Separate supervised ML (predict a known label) from unsupervised (find structure).
Tag anything that reads text from a photo as computer vision or document reading, not NLP.
Mark one rule-based feature as "not AI" and say why it is just logic.
steps.whatItMeans: The exam, and the job, start with naming the workload correctly. The wrong workload means the wrong AWS service and the wrong cost.

steps.title: Write one strength and one limit for each workload
steps.description: Each workload has a strength and a limit, in the team’s own words.
steps.instruction: For each of the five workloads, write one thing it does well and one thing it cannot be trusted to do.
steps.expectedOutput: Each workload has a strength and a limit, in the team’s own words.
steps.whatItMeans: Knowing the limit of a workload is what stops a team from pointing generative AI at a problem that needs a database query.

steps.title: Confirm the Bedrock models for each workload
steps.description: Confirm the Bedrock models for each workload
steps.instruction: List the Bedrock foundation models available, so each generative workload on the map points at a real model you can call.

commands.cmd: aws bedrock list-foundation-models --query "modelSummaries[].modelId" --output table
commands.explain: Lists the foundation model ids available in the region, so each generative workload maps to a callable model.

steps.whatItMeans: Every generative workload on the map has to land on a real model; this is the list those ids come from. Non-generative workloads land on Comprehend, Rekognition or Textract.

outputHighlights.label: A foundation model the studio can call.

fixes.symptom: The list is empty or access denied?
fixes.fix: Request model access once in the Bedrock console under Model access, then re-run.

handoff.note: Your section of the AI Workloads & Capabilities Map, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Read what a foundation model is made of
tasks.objective: See a prompt become tokens and a completion, and read the parts of a model: parameters, context window and temperature.
definitionOfDone: A prompt is shown broken into tokens, with the count
The same prompt is run at two temperatures and the difference recorded
The context-window and parameter size of the local model are recorded

steps.title: Show the model details and its sizes
steps.description: Show the model details and its sizes
steps.instruction: Read the local model’s parameter count and context length from Ollama and record them.

commands.cmd: ollama show llama3.2 | grep -Ei "parameters|context|quantization"
commands.explain: Prints the model’s parameter count, context window and quantization.

steps.expectedOutput:
parameters            3.2B
    context length        131072
    quantization          Q4_K_M
steps.whatItMeans: Parameters are what the model learned; the context window is how much it can read at once. Both decide what it can do and what it costs per call.

outputHighlights.label: How many tokens the model can hold in view at once.

steps.title: Run the same prompt hot and cold
steps.description: Run the same prompt hot and cold
steps.instruction: Run one prompt at temperature 0 and again at temperature 1, and record how the answers differ.

commands.cmd: ollama run llama3.2 --format json <<< '{"prompt":"Name a colour.","options":{"temperature":0}}'; echo "--- now hot ---"; ollama run llama3.2 "Name a colour. Be creative."
commands.explain: The first run is deterministic; the second is free to vary. Compare the two.
commands.sample:
blue
--- now hot ---
How about "vermilion"? It is a vivid reddish-orange.

steps.expectedOutput:
blue
--- now hot ---
How about "vermilion"? It is a vivid reddish-orange.
steps.whatItMeans: Temperature is the one dial that turns a model from a lookup into a brainstorm. For a grounded assistant you want it low.

steps.title: Write the parts in the team’s words
steps.description: Four parts of a model, each explained from the run you just did, not from a textbook.
steps.instruction: In the map, write one plain sentence each for tokens, context window, parameters and temperature, using what you just saw.
steps.expectedOutput: Four parts of a model, each explained from the run you just did, not from a textbook.
steps.whatItMeans: A team that can say what a token and a context window are will not be surprised by a truncated answer or a bill by the token later.

handoff.note: Your section of the AI Workloads & Capabilities Map, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Ground a local model in your notes
tasks.objective: Give the local model a short note and make it answer only from that note, citing it, rather than from memory.
prerequisites: A short plain-text note the model has never seen
definitionOfDone: The model answers a question correctly from the supplied note
The model is shown refusing or hedging when the note does not cover the question
Both runs are saved to the week-1 folder

steps.title: Answer from the note, not from memory
steps.description: Answer from the note, not from memory
steps.instruction: Write a two-line note the model could not know, then ask a question about it with the note pasted in as the only context.

commands.cmd:
printf 'Studio rule: backups run at 02:00 and are kept 30 days.
Ask only about this note.
Question: when do backups run?
' | ollama run llama3.2
commands.explain: Feeds the note plus the question; the answer should come from the note.
commands.sample: Backups run at 02:00, and they are kept for 30 days.

steps.expectedOutput: Backups run at 02:00, and they are kept for 30 days.
steps.whatItMeans: Grounding means the model answers from the text you gave it, so the answer can be checked. This is the whole idea behind the chat app in Week 3.

outputHighlights.label: The answer came from the note, not from training.

steps.title: Catch it when the note does not cover the question
steps.description: Catch it when the note does not cover the question
steps.instruction: Ask the model something the note does not answer, and see whether it admits it or makes something up.

commands.cmd:
printf 'Studio rule: backups run at 02:00 and are kept 30 days.
Answer only from this note; if it is not covered, say so.
Question: what is the restore time?
' | ollama run llama3.2
commands.explain: The note says nothing about restore time; a grounded answer says so rather than inventing a figure.
commands.sample: The note does not say what the restore time is.

steps.expectedOutput: The note does not say what the restore time is.
steps.whatItMeans: A model that invents a restore time is hallucinating. Telling it to answer only from the note, and to say when it cannot, is the cheapest guardrail there is.

fixes.symptom: The model invents a restore time anyway?
fixes.fix: Make the instruction stricter: "If the note does not contain the answer, reply exactly: not in the note." Small models obey a sharp rule better than a soft one.

handoff.note: Your section of the AI Workloads & Capabilities Map, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Assess it against the guidelines
tasks.objective: Walk the assistant through the responsible-AI guidelines and write a finding and a mitigation for each.
definitionOfDone: Each of the six guidelines has a finding specific to this assistant
Each finding has a mitigation the team can actually do
The deployment decision is recorded with the option rejected and the risk accepted

steps.title: Write a finding for each of the six guidelines
steps.description: Six findings, each naming a real risk of this assistant, not a generic sentence.
steps.instruction: For fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency and accountability, write one finding about this specific assistant.
steps.expectedOutput: Six findings, each naming a real risk of this assistant, not a generic sentence.
instructionList: Fairness: who could get a worse answer, and why?
Reliability and safety: what happens when the model is wrong and nobody checks?
Privacy: what data goes into the prompt, and where does it go?
Transparency: does the user know they are talking to an AI, and its limits?
steps.whatItMeans: Responsible AI is a whole domain of the exam and the first question a real customer asks. A finding per guideline turns a slogan into a checklist.

steps.title: Write a mitigation for each finding
steps.description: Six mitigations, each doable this month, each with an owner.
steps.instruction: Beside each finding, write the one mitigation the team will put in place, and who owns it.
steps.expectedOutput: Six mitigations, each doable this month, each with an owner.
steps.whatItMeans: A finding with no mitigation is a complaint. The mitigation and the owner are what turn the assessment into work that gets done.

steps.title: Record the deployment decision
steps.description: A recorded decision with its reason, the rejected option and the accepted risk.
steps.instruction: With the findings in front of the team, record the decision: ship it, ship it with limits, or hold it. Name the option rejected and the risk accepted.
steps.expectedOutput: A recorded decision with its reason, the rejected option and the accepted risk.
steps.whatItMeans: The decision is the drafter’s to make and to own. Writing the rejected option is what proves a choice was made, not defaulted into.

handoff.note: Your section of the Responsible AI Assessment, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Read how it is trained and measured
tasks.objective: See the shape of a training set and a metric, so "accuracy" and "evaluation" mean something concrete.
definitionOfDone: A small labelled set is written, with the label for each row
The model is scored against it and the score recorded
One wrong prediction is read and explained

steps.title: Write a tiny labelled test set
steps.description: Write a tiny labelled test set
steps.instruction: Write five short messages, each labelled spam or ham, as the known-answer set you will score the model against.

commands.cmd:
printf 'win a prize now	spam
lunch at noon?	ham
claim your refund	spam
project due friday	ham
free gift card	spam
' | tee labels.tsv | wc -l
commands.explain: Writes five labelled rows to a file and prints the row count.

steps.whatItMeans: A labelled set is the only thing that turns "it seems good" into a number. Five rows is enough to teach the shape.

outputHighlights.label: Five known answers to score against.

steps.title: Score the model and read a miss
steps.description: Score the model and read a miss
steps.instruction: Ask the model to label each message, compare to the known answer, and count how many it got right.

commands.cmd: while IFS=$'\t' read -r msg want; do got=$(ollama run llama3.2 "Reply with one word, spam or ham: $msg"); printf '%s\twant=%s\tgot=%s\n' "$msg" "$want" "$got"; done < labels.tsv
commands.explain: Runs each row through the model and prints the wanted vs the predicted label.
commands.sample:
win a prize now	want=spam	got=spam
lunch at noon?	want=ham	got=ham
claim your refund	want=spam	got=spam
project due friday	want=ham	got=ham
free gift card	want=spam	got=spam

steps.expectedOutput:
win a prize now	want=spam	got=spam
lunch at noon?	want=ham	got=ham
claim your refund	want=spam	got=spam
project due friday	want=ham	got=ham
free gift card	want=spam	got=spam
steps.whatItMeans: This is evaluation in miniature: a prediction beside a known answer. Accuracy is just how many of these lines match.

fixes.symptom: The model replies with a sentence, not one word?
fixes.fix: Tighten the prompt: "Reply with exactly one word: spam or ham." Record that prompt change as part of the result.

handoff.note: Your section of the Responsible AI Assessment, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Work a wrong answer until it is grounded
tasks.objective: Take an answer the model got wrong and work it the method way: one theory, one change, one result per row, until it is grounded.
prerequisites: A model answer that is wrong or ungrounded, from Week 1 or 2
definitionOfDone: The wrong answer is written exactly, before any theory
Every attempt is a row: theory, the one change, the result
At least one theory was wrong and the row says so
The fixed answer is grounded and cites the note

steps.title: Write the wrong answer exactly
steps.description: The log opens with the prompt, the wrong answer and why it is wrong, and no theory yet.
steps.instruction: Before any theory, write the prompt, the answer the model gave, and exactly why it is wrong or ungrounded.
steps.expectedOutput: The log opens with the prompt, the wrong answer and why it is wrong, and no theory yet.
steps.whatItMeans: The method starts with the symptom written down. For an AI answer the symptom is the exact wrong output, not "it seems off".

steps.title: Change one thing per row and record the result
steps.description: Change one thing per row and record the result
steps.instruction: Write one theory for why it is wrong, change exactly one thing to test it, and record the result. A wrong theory gets its own row.

commands.cmd: ollama run llama3.2 "Answer only from this note; if missing, say not in the note. Note: backups run 02:00. Q: when do backups run?"
commands.explain: Tests one theory: the earlier answer drifted because the instruction was loose. Tighten it and re-run.

steps.expectedOutput: Backups run at 02:00.
steps.whatItMeans: One change per row is what makes the log trustworthy: you can always say which change fixed it. The same method A+ uses on hardware.

outputHighlights.label: The tightened instruction grounded the answer.

fixes.symptom: Changing the prompt did not help?
fixes.fix: Change the next single thing: add the note to context, or lower temperature. One change per row.

steps.title: Record the grounded answer and the failed theories
steps.description: The log ends with a grounded, cited answer and keeps every theory that failed on the way.
steps.instruction: Write the final grounded answer, confirm it cites the note, and keep the rows for the theories that did not work.
steps.expectedOutput: The log ends with a grounded, cited answer and keeps every theory that failed on the way.
steps.whatItMeans: A log with no failed theories in it is a log nobody believes. The failures are the proof the team actually worked the problem.

handoff.note: Your section of the Evaluation & Grounding Log, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Invoke a model on Bedrock
tasks.objective: Request model access, invoke a Bedrock foundation model once from the shell, and record the model id.
prerequisites: The AWS free account with a budget alert (Week 0)
definitionOfDone: Model access is granted for one foundation model
The model answers one InvokeModel call from the shell
The model id is recorded and no secret is pasted into the record

cost.note: On-demand calls kept tiny; a cent or two at most, torn down at the end.

steps.title: Request access to a foundation model
steps.description: One foundation model shows Access granted in the Bedrock console.
steps.instruction: In the Bedrock console, open Model access and request access to one small text model.
steps.expectedOutput: One foundation model shows Access granted in the Bedrock console.
instructionList: Open Bedrock in a region that offers the model you want.
Request access to a small text model such as Amazon Titan Text or Claude Haiku.
Access is usually instant; note the exact model id, you call it by that.
steps.whatItMeans: Bedrock is serverless: there is no endpoint to stand up, only access to request and a model id to call. That is the AWS way to reach a foundation model.

steps.title: Invoke the model once
steps.description: Invoke the model once
steps.instruction: Send one prompt to the model through the Bedrock runtime and read the completion back.

commands.cmd: aws bedrock-runtime invoke-model --model-id amazon.titan-text-express-v1 --body '{"inputText":"In one word, name a colour."}' --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out /dev/stdout | head -c 200
commands.explain: Calls the model once and prints the start of its JSON response.

steps.expectedOutput: {"inputTextTokenCount":7,"results":[{"tokenCount":2,"outputText":"Blue","completionReason":"FINISH"}]}
steps.whatItMeans: A single InvokeModel call that returns outputText is the proof the model is reachable and callable before any app is written against it.

outputHighlights.label: The model answered through the runtime.

fixes.symptom: AccessDeniedException?
fixes.fix: Model access is not granted yet, or the IAM user lacks bedrock:InvokeModel. Grant access and the policy, then re-run.

fixes.symptom: ValidationException on the body?
fixes.fix: The body shape differs per model family; check the model’s request format in the Bedrock docs.

handoff.note: Your section of the Bedrock Build Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Build a grounded chat app
tasks.objective: Write a tiny chat client that answers only from the studio documents, the grounding you proved locally in Week 1.
prerequisites: Bedrock model access (this week) or the local model (Week 0) as a fallback
definitionOfDone: The app answers a question from the studio documents
The app says when the documents do not cover a question
The transcript is saved to the week-3 folder

cost.note: Falls back to the free local model if Bedrock access is not ready.

steps.title: Answer from the documents
steps.description: Answer from the documents
steps.instruction: Run the chat client with a studio document as context and ask a question it answers.

commands.cmd: python chat.py --grounding studio-notes.txt --ask "when do backups run?"
commands.explain: Loads the document as the only context and answers from it, via Bedrock or the local model.
commands.sample: Backups run at 02:00 and are kept for 30 days. [source: studio-notes.txt]

steps.expectedOutput: Backups run at 02:00 and are kept for 30 days. [source: studio-notes.txt]
steps.whatItMeans: A grounded app is just the Week 1 trick wired up: the document goes in the context, the model answers from it, and the answer cites it.

outputHighlights.label: The answer cites the document it came from.

fixes.symptom: No Bedrock access yet?
fixes.fix: Point the client at the local Ollama model; the grounding logic is identical.

steps.title: Refuse when the documents are silent
steps.description: Refuse when the documents are silent
steps.instruction: Ask the app something the documents do not cover and confirm it declines rather than inventing an answer.

commands.cmd: python chat.py --grounding studio-notes.txt --ask "what is the office wifi password?"
commands.explain: The documents do not cover this; a grounded app says so.
commands.sample: That is not covered in the studio documents.

steps.expectedOutput: That is not covered in the studio documents.
steps.whatItMeans: The refusal is the feature. An assistant that admits what it does not know is one a customer can trust with the answers it does give.

handoff.note: Your section of the Bedrock Build Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Add language and document reading
tasks.objective: Call a language service and a document service, so the assistant can read sentiment and read text out of a scan.
prerequisites: An AWS account with Comprehend and Textract available
definitionOfDone: A Comprehend call returns sentiment for a sentence
A Textract call returns the text read out of a document
Both responses are saved to the week-3 folder

cost.note: Comprehend and Textract free tiers cover the course calls.

steps.title: Read sentiment from a sentence
steps.description: Read sentiment from a sentence
steps.instruction: Send one sentence to Amazon Comprehend and read back its sentiment.

commands.cmd: aws comprehend detect-sentiment --text "The studio handover was clear and fast." --language-code en --query "Sentiment" --output text
commands.explain: Classifies the sentiment of the sentence and prints the single label.

KPIS.numerator: Blind peer reviews the member completed.
KPIS.denominator: Peer reviews assigned to the member.
KPIS.whyMember: Reviews of other teams’ frozen work, answered question by question.
KPIS.whyCompany: Review work done for others, from the blind review queue.

KPIS.label: Teammate steps ticked

KPIS.whyCompany: Help given across roles, counted in steps.

KPIS.label: On time
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose last verification fell on or before the week due date.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with a verification; needs the cohort start date.

KPIS.whyCompany: Reliability against a calendar, read from the verification stamps and the cohort start.

KPIS.label: Document control complete
KPIS.numerator: Forms with data whose document-control block is complete.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role with data.
KPIS.whyMember: Id, version, owner, date and status on every document the team filled.
KPIS.whyCompany: Document control kept on every filled form: id, version, owner, date, status.

KPIS.label: Controls cited
KPIS.numerator: Distinct control codes on approved or issued forms the role drafts.
KPIS.denominator: Distinct control codes the forms of the role cite.
KPIS.whyMember: The published controls the approved documents cite, by code.
KPIS.whyCompany: Control codes practised through approved documents, by standard.

KPIS.label: Instructor approved
KPIS.numerator: Forms of the role whose latest instructor review is approved.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Forms an instructor reviewed and approved; the latest review per form counts.
KPIS.whyCompany: Forms with an instructor verdict of approved, the latest review per form.

KPIS.label: Skills proved twice
KPIS.numerator: Skills with verified steps on two or more distinct tasks.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: A skill verified on two different tasks was carried from one context to another.
KPIS.whyCompany: Verification repeated on a second task is harder to reach by luck or by copying.

KPIS.label: Skills retained
KPIS.numerator: Skills verified again seven or more days after their first verification.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: Proof a week or more apart: the skill stayed.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention read from the gap between two verification stamps on the same skill.

KPIS.label: Learning velocity
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those; the percentage caps at one hundred.
KPIS.whyMember: This month against last: rising, level or slowing, from the verification stamps.
KPIS.whyCompany: Pace of verified work, month on month, from recorded stamps.

KPIS.label: Profile coverage
KPIS.numerator: Required competencies of the selected work role or environment profile at verified or better.
KPIS.denominator: Required competencies the selected work role or environment profile names.
KPIS.whyMember: Measures the verified skills against a job role or a published company profile, with the untaught gap named.
KPIS.whyCompany: Coverage of the competencies a work role or an environment profile requires, read from verified steps.

KPIS.label: Values recalled
KPIS.numerator: Recall activities answered correctly: the value the team recorded, picked among distractors.
KPIS.denominator: Recall activities answered, from the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Weeks after recording an address, a prefix, a port or a decision, the member still knows it.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention of the project the member built, read from answers given without the form open.

KPIS.label: Scenarios applied
KPIS.numerator: Applied scenarios answered correctly: an address inside the prefix, a free port on the host, the committed size.
KPIS.denominator: Applied scenarios offered at the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Takes a value the team recorded and uses it under a change the course did not script.
KPIS.whyCompany: Applied use of recorded facts, not recall alone; offered scenarios count whether or not answered.

KPIS.label: Conflicts resolved
KPIS.numerator: Conflicts the record found that the team resolved: the address, the port, the prefix, the size no longer at odds.
KPIS.denominator: Conflicts the record found at the checkpoints reached, resolved or still open.
KPIS.whyMember: A duplicate address or an over-committed host found by the platform and fixed by the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Contradictions in the record closed, read from the record itself rather than from a claim.

KPIS.label: Minutes on task
KPIS.numerator: Whole minutes the member had tasks of this course open on a visible tab, pauses excluded.
KPIS.denominator: A count; nothing is read into it.
KPIS.whyMember: How long the work took the member, by the timer they can pause; measured, never rewarded.
KPIS.whyCompany: Time on task as context for the other rows; no score reads it.

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Technical capability
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: What the member can do: skills, commands and procedures proven by output against the exam and the role.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Can this member operate the tools and run the procedures the job needs?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Problem solving
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Faults logged and resolved, verifications reached after a failed paste, stuck flags cleared, and the minutes between first paste and proof.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: When something breaks, does this member find and fix it, and how long does it take?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Professional execution
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: How the work was done: steps in order, first pastes, evidence named to convention, every check due met.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member follow the runbook as written and leave evidence an auditor can find?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Decision making
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options, justified, approved by the team, and changes with a rollback written.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Teamwork
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given and steps ticked on teammates’ tasks.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly and hold their lane in a team?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Professionalism
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, documents controlled, controls cited, instructor approval earned.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member deliver on time, to standard, and to the reviewer’s satisfaction?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Growth
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Skills proved twice, retained across weeks, verified faster week on week, and the gap to a work role closing.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Understanding
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Values the team recorded, recalled and applied weeks later; conflicts the record found, resolved; minutes on task, measured.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Did this member retain what the team built, and can they apply it when something changes?

PRACTICES.label: Hash evidence at capture
PRACTICES.definition: Every artifact is hashed when it is saved and the digest is recorded, so later copies can be checked.

PRACTICES.label: Retest to closure
PRACTICES.definition: A finding is closed only by a retest that shows the fix, and every finding ends Closed, Open or Risk accepted.

PRACTICES.label: Likelihood-times-impact scoring
PRACTICES.definition: Each risk is scored on a stated scale for likelihood and impact, and the score decides the order.

PRACTICES.label: Configuration record
PRACTICES.definition: Every device configuration is saved, versioned and compared after a change.

PRACTICES.label: Build record
PRACTICES.definition: A build is recorded step by step with firmware, versions and settings as it is made.

PRACTICES.label: Software bill of materials
PRACTICES.definition: A release lists its components (CycloneDX or SPDX), so a vulnerable dependency can be found.

PRACTICES.label: Guardrail regression tests
PRACTICES.definition: Every blocked attack case becomes a test the pipeline runs, so a removed guardrail fails the build.

PRACTICES.label: Budget guardrails
PRACTICES.definition: A budget with alerts is set before the first resource, and the alert is tested.

PRACTICES.label: Sign and version documents
PRACTICES.definition: A document carries an id, a version, an owner, a date and a status, and a change makes a new version.

PRACTICES.label: As-built documentation
PRACTICES.definition: What was actually built is recorded, with addresses, versions and owners, and handed over with the system.

PRACTICES.label: Architecture decision records
PRACTICES.definition: Each significant design choice is recorded with its context, options and consequences.

PRACTICES.label: Test and acceptance
PRACTICES.definition: A build is accepted against written tests with recorded results, not against a feeling that it works.

PRACTICES.label: Evidence by design
PRACTICES.definition: Every control names the evidence that proves it operates, and the evidence is collected as the work happens.

PRACTICES.label: Least privilege for agents
PRACTICES.definition: An agent or tool call holds a scoped credential and no admin right, and its actions are logged.

PRACTICES.label: Redact before write
PRACTICES.definition: Personal data is detected and removed before a prompt, a log or a dataset is stored.

PRACTICES.label: Human checkpoint

SCORING.label: Collaboration
SCORING.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected and peer reviews given, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Team facts count for the team; the role share on the KPIs says what this member moved.

SCORING.label: Reliability
SCORING.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, document control complete, controls cited and instructor approval, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: On time needs the cohort start date; without one the score stands on the other three and says so.

SCORING.label: Readiness
SCORING.definition: Exam weight verified, work-role coverage, skills retained and steps in order, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: A reading of the record against an exam and a work role, not a prediction of a pass or a hire.

SCORING.label: Understanding retained
SCORING.definition: Values recalled, scenarios applied and conflicts resolved, weeks after the team recorded them, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Asks only about values the team recorded; before the checkpoint week the score stands on nothing and says so.

STANDARDS.label: NIST CSF
STANDARDS.description: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
STANDARDS.why: Organises all security work into six functions. Tagging a step here shows which part of the lifecycle it strengthens and proves the work covered the whole picture, not just attack or defence.

STANDARDS.label: CIS
STANDARDS.description: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 and the CIS Benchmarks
STANDARDS.why: A prioritised "do these first" list of safeguards. A CIS tag means this step implements an industry-baseline control that auditors and blue teams recognise at once.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-61
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-61 Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
STANDARDS.why: The incident-handling playbook: prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. This tag means the step is part of a defensible, court-ready incident response process.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-115
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-115 Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
STANDARDS.why: The standard method for security testing and assessment. Following it makes scanning and exploitation repeatable, authorised and credible in a report.

STANDARDS.label: ISO 27001
STANDARDS.why: The certifiable information security management standard. This tag means the step produces the documented policy or evidence an ISO 27001 audit expects to see.

STANDARDS.label: SOC 2
STANDARDS.description: AICPA Trust Services Criteria for a SOC 2 examination
STANDARDS.why: The AICPA attestation standard built on the Trust Services Criteria: Security is CC1 to CC9, plus Availability, Confidentiality and the rest. This tag means the step produces a control or the evidence a SOC 2 Type I or II examiner samples.

STANDARDS.label: ITIL 4
STANDARDS.description: ITIL 4 service management practices: change, incident, problem, release
STANDARDS.why: The operating disciplines a network team is judged on: change, incident and problem management. A tag here means the step is not just technically right but done the way an organisation can audit: requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded.

STANDARDS.label: Well-Architected
STANDARDS.description: Well-Architected Framework pillars, Azure and AWS
STANDARDS.why: Both clouds judge a design on the same pillars: reliability, security, cost, operational excellence and performance. A tag here means the step is a design choice one of them would ask about.

STANDARDS.label: NIST AI RMF
STANDARDS.description: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and its Generative AI Profile
STANDARDS.why: The AI framework Ridgeline adopts: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. A tag here means the step produces something an AI risk register or the AI questions a buyer asks will ask for.

STANDARDS.label: OWASP LLM Top 10
STANDARDS.description: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
STANDARDS.why: The shared catalogue of LLM application weaknesses: prompt injection, sensitive disclosure, excessive agency and the rest. A tag here names the weakness the step attacks or defends.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 42001
STANDARDS.why: The certifiable management system standard for AI. Customers ask about it; a tag here means the step produces the kind of record an AI management system keeps.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-53
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security and privacy controls
STANDARDS.why: The federal control catalogue the sixteen CISSP control statements are drawn from (PM-1, SC-7, AC-2). A tag here means the step writes or proves one of those controls.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-30
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-30 Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments
STANDARDS.why: The federal method for a risk assessment: threat sources, events, likelihood and impact. A risk register that follows it can be defended line by line.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-218
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
STANDARDS.why: The practices a secure software pipeline follows: protect the code, produce well-secured software, respond to vulnerabilities. A pipeline record that cites it names the gate each practice became.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27005
STANDARDS.why: The risk method behind ISO 27001 clause 6: identify, analyse, evaluate, treat. A risk register that cites it reads the same way to an auditor.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27037
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27037 identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence
STANDARDS.why: How evidence is collected and kept so it still counts later: identify, collect, acquire, preserve, with a chain of custody. An evidence log that cites it can be trusted in a dispute.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010
STANDARDS.why: What an architecture description must contain: stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints and the decisions behind them. A solution architecture document that cites it is complete rather than a diagram.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).

glossary.data.src_ip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a network (Suricata) alert — who the traffic came from.
glossary.data.srcip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a host alert (logins, web requests). Its network twin is data.src_ip — search both.
glossary.ossec.conf: The Wazuh agent's config file. It names the SOC to report to and any extra log files to ship.
glossary.hydra: A password-guessing tool. In this lab you run it against your own pod so the SOC has a brute-force attack to detect.
glossary.tcpdump: A command-line tool that records network traffic to a .pcap file you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.Wireshark: A traffic viewer. Open a .pcap in it and "Follow HTTP Stream" to read the exact request an attacker sent.
glossary.Kali: The attacker machine in your lab — a Linux build that ships with nmap, nikto, hydra and the rest.
glossary.Proxmox: A hypervisor — an operating system whose job is to run virtual machines. In Server+ you install it on your own server; in the CySA lab it already runs the lab.
glossary.POST: Power-On Self-Test — the hardware check a machine runs the moment you power it on, before any operating system. Beeps and blink codes are POST talking to you.
glossary.DIMM: A memory stick. Which slots they go in is dictated by the motherboard manual, and the wrong slots can stop the machine starting at all.
glossary.ECC: Error-Correcting Code memory — server RAM that detects and fixes single-bit corruption on the fly. Servers use it; desktops usually do not.
glossary.HCL: Hardware Compatibility List — the check that the software you plan to run officially supports the exact hardware you have, before you build on it.
glossary.UEFI: The modern replacement for the old BIOS firmware. Boot mode matters: an OS installed under UEFI will not boot if the firmware is later switched to legacy.
glossary.IOMMU: The chip feature (Intel VT-d / AMD-Vi) that lets a virtual machine be handed a real piece of hardware, like a NIC, as its own.
glossary.VT-x: Intel’s virtualization extensions. Present is not enough — they must be ENABLED in firmware setup, or the hypervisor cannot start a single VM.
glossary.stripe size: How large a chunk of data a RAID array writes to one disk before moving to the next. The default is right for this build.
glossary.IDS: Intrusion Detection System — software that watches traffic and raises an alert when it matches a known attack pattern. Suricata is yours.
glossary.NVD: National Vulnerability Database — the public catalogue you search to find a CVE and its score for a given software version.
glossary.pod: Your team’s pair of machines: one Ubuntu web server and one Windows PC.
glossary.escalate: Pass an alert on for deeper investigation, with the reason written down, instead of closing it yourself.
glossary.SOC: Security Operations Centre — the team (and dashboard) that watches for attacks around the clock.
glossary.SIEM: Security Information and Event Management — software that gathers logs from everywhere and raises alerts. Wazuh is your SIEM.
glossary.IOC: Indicator of Compromise — a clue an attacker leaves behind, like a bad IP address, file name, or hash.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public ID for one specific known software flaw, e.g. CVE-2021-41773.
glossary.CVSS: A 0–10 score for how severe a vulnerability is, so you can rank what to fix first.
glossary.pcap: A 'packet capture' — a saved recording of network traffic you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.SQLi: SQL injection — tricking a website into running database commands it shouldn't, often to steal data.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall — a filter in front of a website that blocks common attacks like SQL injection.
glossary.POA&M: Plan of Action & Milestones — a to-do list for fixing findings: what, who owns it, and by when.
glossary.PTES: Penetration Testing Execution Standard — the agreed steps of a pentest: recon, scan, exploit, report.
glossary.STRIDE: A checklist of threat types: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
glossary.NIC: Network Interface Card — a machine's network connection. On these VMs it's usually named ens18.
glossary.IaC: Infrastructure as Code — describing machines in a text file a tool applies, so the build is repeatable and the file is the record. Terraform or OpenTofu is yours.
glossary.OpenTofu: The open-source fork of Terraform, kept under the Linux Foundation after HashiCorp changed Terraform’s licence in 2023. Same HCL, same providers, same state files; the command is tofu instead of terraform.
glossary.exporter: A small program on a host that publishes its metrics on an HTTP port for Prometheus to collect. node_exporter for Linux, windows_exporter for Windows.
glossary.IPAM: IP Address Management — the tool that holds every subnet and address and who has it, so the plan and reality are the same document. NetBox is yours.
glossary.FIM: File Integrity Monitoring — an agent that hashes important files and alerts when one changes, which is how a tampered config gets noticed.
glossary.cloud-init: The first-boot setup a cloud image runs: hostname, user, keys and addressing handed in from outside, so a clone comes up configured instead of blank.
glossary.DNAT: Destination NAT — the host rewriting where a packet is going. The rule that turns a request to the host’s campus address on port 80 into a request to websrv in the DMZ.
glossary.MASQUERADE: Source NAT behind the host’s own address, so a reply from the campus LAN or the internet comes back to the host and is handed to the guest that asked.
glossary.published port: A port on the host’s campus address that a DNAT rule hands to a VM behind it. Each one is a deliberate hole in the segmentation, and you should be able to say why it exists.
glossary.idempotent: Running it twice gives the same result as running it once. The property that makes a playbook safe to run every night — and why changed=0 on the second run is the proof.
glossary.drift: Reality diverging from what the code says — a change made in the console instead of the repository. terraform plan (tofu plan) detects it; the next apply may undo it.
glossary.dynamic inventory: Ansible asking the hypervisor which hosts exist instead of reading a list someone typed. The list is never out of date because there is no list.
glossary.XDR: Extended Detection and Response — one platform watching endpoints, logs and files across a whole fleet. Wazuh on the Core is the MSP’s.
glossary.verify job: The backup server re-reading a backup, chunk by chunk, to confirm it is restorable before anyone needs it.
glossary.SLO: Service Level Objective — the availability you promise a client, as a number. The SLA is the contract around it.
glossary.SCA: Security Configuration Assessment — checking a machine's settings against a hardening benchmark.
glossary.Rules of Engagement: The written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.RoE: Rules of Engagement — the written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.triage: Quickly sorting alerts into real vs noise and deciding what to escalate — like an ER nurse.
glossary.baseline: A record of what 'normal' looks like, so you can spot what's abnormal later.
glossary.chain of custody: A documented trail of who handled each piece of evidence and when — so it holds up as proof.
glossary.agent: A small program installed on each machine that ships its logs to the SOC.
glossary.gate: A checkpoint at the end of a week — finish its required work before the next week unlocks.
glossary.eve.json: The file where Suricata writes its network alerts.
glossary.subnet: A slice of a network sharing an address range, e.g. 10.10.100.x.
glossary.Wazuh: The free, open-source SIEM/SOC platform this lab is built on.
glossary.Suricata: An open-source network intrusion detector that watches traffic and raises alerts.
glossary.Sysmon: A Windows tool that records detailed activity — processes, connections, file changes.
glossary.DVWA: Damn Vulnerable Web App — a deliberately insecure web app used as a safe attack target.
glossary.nmap: A scanner that finds open ports and what software is running on them.
glossary.nikto: A scanner that checks a web server for known issues.
glossary.MITRE ATT&CK: A public catalogue of attacker techniques, used to describe how an attack was carried out.
glossary.MTTD: Mean Time To Detect — the average time from an attack starting to it being noticed.
glossary.MTTR: Mean Time To Respond — the average time from detecting an attack to containing it.
glossary.rule.level: Wazuh scores every alert 0–15 by severity; searching rule.level:>=7 keeps the ones that usually matter.
glossary.rule.groups: The category tags Wazuh puts on an alert (e.g. authentication_failed, ids, web) — handy for filtering by attack type.
glossary.agent.name: The Wazuh field naming which machine an alert came from (e.g. Team07-ubuntu) — use it to filter to one host.
glossary.event channel: A named Windows log stream — Sysmon writes to Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational, which the agent forwards.
glossary.Emerging Threats ruleset: The community alert rules Suricata downloads with suricata-update — without them it sees traffic but raises nothing.
glossary.DQL: Dashboard Query Language — the field:value search syntax in the Wazuh/OpenSearch search bar (e.g. data.src_ip:10.10.30.7).
glossary.Discover: The Wazuh/OpenSearch view that lists raw events in a table you can search, add columns to, and save.
glossary.time picker: The date/time control (top-right) that sets which window of events you see — the #1 reason a correct search looks empty.
glossary.visualization: A saved chart (bar, pie, table) built from a search — the building block you drop onto a dashboard.
glossary.dashboard: A saved page of visualizations and searches you assemble to watch at a glance.
glossary.rule.description: The Wazuh field holding the human-readable name of the rule that fired — useful to group and count alerts by.
glossary.syscheck: Wazuh’s File Integrity Monitoring engine; its events carry syscheck.path and whether a file was added/modified/deleted.
glossary.sensor: A program on a machine that watches activity and reports it to the SOC — your Wazuh agent, Suricata and Sysmon are all sensors.
glossary.endpoint: Any individual computer on the network — a laptop, server or VM — as opposed to the network gear between them.
glossary.telemetry: The stream of activity data a machine sends about itself — processes, logins, connections — that the SOC watches.
glossary.hash: A short fingerprint calculated from a file; change one byte and the fingerprint changes, so it proves the file was not tampered with.
glossary.hashing: Running a file through a formula to get its fixed-length fingerprint (its hash).
glossary.SHA-256: A widely trusted hashing method that turns any file into a 64-character fingerprint.
glossary.false positive: An alert that turned out to be harmless — the tool flagged something that was not actually an attack.
glossary.true positive: An alert that was real — the flagged activity really was malicious.
glossary.enroll: To register a machine with the SOC so its agent starts sending logs.
glossary.brute force: Guessing a password by automatically trying huge numbers of combinations until one works.
glossary.port scan: Probing a machine to list which network ports are open, to discover what services it is running.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell — a way to log in to and run commands on another machine over the network, from your terminal.
glossary.pivot: To follow a clue (like an IP or username) from one log into related events, tracing an attacker’s movements.
glossary.hardening: Making a machine harder to attack by closing unused services, fixing weak settings and applying updates.
glossary.containment: Stopping an attack from spreading — e.g. isolating the affected machine — once you have detected it.
glossary.vulnerability: A weakness in software or configuration that an attacker could exploit.
glossary.vuln: Short for vulnerability — a weakness an attacker could exploit.
glossary.firewall: A filter that allows or blocks network connections by rule, to keep unwanted traffic out.
glossary.ufw: Uncomplicated Firewall — the simple command-line firewall on Ubuntu (e.g. ufw allow 22).
glossary.VLAN: A virtual LAN — one physical switch split into separate networks. Ports in different VLANs cannot talk without something routing between them, which is the whole point.
glossary.trunk: A link between switches that carries several VLANs at once, tagging each frame with its VLAN id (802.1Q). The alternative is one cable per VLAN.
glossary.native VLAN: The one VLAN a trunk carries UNTAGGED. If the two ends disagree about which it is, traffic silently lands in the wrong network — the classic trunk fault.
glossary.SVI: Switched Virtual Interface — a VLAN’s gateway configured on the switch itself. A switch with SVIs routes between VLANs at wire speed; a switch without them needs a router.
glossary.router-on-a-stick: Inter-VLAN routing done by a router over a single trunk, with one subinterface per VLAN. What you build when the switch cannot route — same outcome, one link carrying all of it.
glossary.EtherChannel: Two or more physical links bundled into one logical link, so a cable can fail without an outage and the bandwidth adds up. LACP is the protocol that negotiates it.
glossary.spanning tree: The protocol that stops a loop when switches have more than one path between them, by blocking all but one. It always picks a root switch — set it deliberately or it picks the oldest one.
glossary.PortFast: Tells spanning tree an access port has a PC on it, not a switch, so it forwards immediately instead of waiting. Never on a port that could reach another switch.
glossary.BPDU Guard: Shuts a PortFast port the moment it hears spanning-tree messages — which means somebody plugged a switch into a desk port. The protection that makes PortFast safe.
glossary.OSPF: A routing protocol: routers tell each other which networks they can reach, so each works out its own routes. It replaces static routes and reacts when a link dies.
glossary.OSPF area: A grouping that limits how far routing detail spreads. This course uses a single area 0 — the backbone — because one correctly adjacent area is the CCNA outcome.
glossary.adjacency: Two OSPF routers that have agreed to exchange routes. It has to reach the FULL state; anything less is the protocol telling you what does not match.
glossary.NAT: Network Address Translation — rewriting addresses as traffic crosses the edge, so internal addresses that mean nothing on the internet can still reach it.
glossary.PAT: Port Address Translation, sometimes "NAT overload" — the whole company sharing one public address, told apart by port number. What almost every small site actually runs.
glossary.ACL: Access Control List — an ordered list of permit and deny rules applied to an interface in one direction. It ends with an implicit deny, which is why the order matters.
glossary.port security: Limits which or how many MAC addresses a switch port accepts, so a stranger plugging into a desk port cannot quietly join the network.
glossary.ip helper-address: Tells a router to forward DHCP requests from a VLAN to a DHCP server somewhere else. The enterprise pattern, versus the router serving DHCP itself.
glossary.SNMP: The protocol a monitoring system uses to read a device’s interfaces, CPU and memory. Read-only is all a NOC needs; v3 is the version with real authentication.
glossary.syslog: Device log messages sent to a central collector. With synchronised clocks it turns "it broke this morning" into a readable sequence across every device.
glossary.NetBox: The source of truth for the network: sites, devices, interfaces, cables, VLANs and prefixes, with an API. It replaces the spreadsheet once the spreadsheet stops scaling.
glossary.Oxidized: Collects every device’s configuration on a schedule and commits it to Git, so you have both a backup and a history of what changed.
glossary.source of truth: The one system that DEFINES what the network should be. Tools read from it and configure devices to match, so the documentation cannot drift from reality.
glossary.PoE: Power over Ethernet — the switch powering the device on the far end of the cable, which is how phones and access points run without a plug of their own.
glossary.SFP: The slot a fibre (or copper) transceiver plugs into, for uplinks that go further or faster than the built-in ports.
glossary.resource group: Azure’s folder for resources. Everything in it shares a lifecycle: delete the group and everything inside goes with it.
glossary.VNet: Virtual network — your own private network inside Azure, with an address range you choose. AWS calls it a VPC.
glossary.VPC: Virtual Private Cloud — your own private network inside AWS, with an address range you choose. Azure calls it a VNet.
glossary.NSG: Network security group — Azure’s firewall rule set for a subnet or a network card. Rules are checked by priority, lowest number first.
glossary.security group: AWS’s firewall around an instance. It only has allow rules: anything not allowed is blocked, and replies to allowed traffic are let back in automatically.
glossary.CIDR: The slash notation for an address range: 10.10.0.0/16 means the first 16 bits are fixed, leaving 65,536 addresses. /24 leaves 256.
glossary.RFC 1918: The three private address ranges (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x) that never route on the public internet, so every company can reuse them.
glossary.RBAC: Role-based access control — Azure’s way of granting access: a person or group gets a role (Reader, Contributor, Owner) at a scope (subscription, group, resource).
glossary.IAM: Identity and Access Management — AWS’s service for users, groups, roles and the policies that say what each may do.
glossary.managed identity: An identity Azure gives a resource (like a Function) so it can sign in to other services with no password or key stored anywhere.
glossary.IAM role: An identity a service (like a Lambda function or an EC2 instance) assumes to get short-lived credentials — the AWS equivalent of a managed identity.
glossary.tags: Key=value labels on a resource (owner=team01-infra). They carry what a name cannot: who to ask, which environment, which cost centre.
glossary.$5 budget: A spending limit with alerts. It does not stop spending by itself — it emails you before a mistake becomes expensive.
glossary.TLS 1.2: The minimum modern version of the encryption behind HTTPS. Older versions have known weaknesses, so servers are told to refuse them.
glossary.SSH key: A key pair for signing in to a Linux machine: the public half goes on the server, the private half stays with you. No password exists to guess.
glossary.key pair: AWS’s name for an SSH key pair. The private .pem file is shown once at creation — download it and keep it out of the repository.
glossary.deallocate: Stop an Azure VM so its compute is released and stops billing. A shutdown from inside the OS leaves it “stopped” but still allocated and still paid for.
glossary.public IP: An internet-routable address on a resource. It is what the outside world (and your SSH test) reaches; the private IP is what other resources use.
glossary.IMDSv2: The token-based version of the instance metadata service on EC2. Requiring it blocks a common trick that steals an instance’s credentials.
glossary.static website: A site made of plain files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) served straight from storage — no web server to run or patch.
glossary.S3: Simple Storage Service — AWS object storage. A bucket holds files; the name is unique across all of AWS.
glossary.CloudFront: AWS’s content delivery network. It sits in front of the bucket, serves the site over HTTPS, and caches copies near visitors.
glossary.OAC: Origin Access Control — the setting that lets CloudFront read a private bucket on your behalf, so the bucket itself never becomes public.
glossary.serverless: Code or a database you pay for per request, with no server to size, patch or switch off. Idle means free.
glossary.Consumption plan: The Azure Functions plan that bills per execution and scales to zero. The first million executions a month are free.
glossary.Lambda: AWS’s serverless code service: upload a function, it runs when triggered, and you pay per call.
glossary.API Gateway: The AWS front door for an API: it gives your function an HTTPS URL and handles CORS.
glossary.Cosmos DB: Azure’s globally distributed NoSQL database. In serverless mode it bills per request unit used.
glossary.DynamoDB: AWS’s NoSQL key-value database. On-demand mode bills per request; 25 GB is always free.
glossary.partition key: The field a NoSQL database uses to decide where an item is stored. Chosen at creation, and cannot be changed later.
glossary.binding: An Azure Functions shortcut that connects a function to a service (like Cosmos DB) through configuration, so the code never opens a connection itself.
glossary.CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — the browser rule that lets a page from one site read an API’s answer only if the API lists that site as an allowed origin.
glossary.allowed origin: The scheme, host and port of a page (https://mysite.example). CORS decides per origin which pages may read an API.
glossary.Application Insights: Azure’s application monitoring: every request, failure and exception from the Function, searchable.
glossary.CloudWatch: AWS’s monitoring service: logs, metrics and alarms in one place.
glossary.action group: Azure’s “who gets told and how” list. Alerts point at it, so the email address changes in one place.
glossary.SNS: Simple Notification Service — AWS’s “who gets told” topic. Alarms publish to it; email subscribers must confirm once.
glossary.Key Vault: Azure’s safe for secrets, keys and certificates. An app setting can point at a secret instead of holding it.
glossary.Cost Explorer: AWS’s cost report. Must be enabled once and takes up to a day to fill; the console view is free, the API is not.
glossary.Free Tier: What AWS gives away: some things for 12 months after the account opens (750 EC2 hours a month), some always (Lambda, DynamoDB).
glossary.Cloud Shell: A terminal in the browser with the Azure CLI signed in already. It needs a small storage share the first time.
glossary.CloudShell: A terminal in the browser with the AWS CLI signed in already. Free.
glossary.shared responsibility: Who secures what: the provider runs the datacenter, hardware and (for PaaS) the platform; you own your data, identities, configuration and — on a VM — the operating system.
glossary.IaaS: Infrastructure as a Service — you rent a machine and network and manage the operating system yourself. A VM is IaaS.
glossary.PaaS: Platform as a Service — you bring code and data; the provider runs and patches the platform. Functions, a static website and a managed database are PaaS.
glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service — a finished application you sign in to, like Microsoft 365 or the GitHub website.
glossary.availability zone: One of several separate datacenters inside a region, with its own power and cooling. Two zones fail independently; one region can still fail as a whole.
glossary.resource lock: An Azure setting on a resource or group that refuses deletes (CanNotDelete) or any change (ReadOnly) until someone removes the lock first.
glossary.Advisor: Azure’s free recommendation service: cost, security, reliability, performance and operational tips for what you have deployed.
glossary.Service Health: Azure’s page for incidents and planned maintenance that affect your subscription’s regions and services.
glossary.Trusted Advisor: AWS’s free checks for cost, security, fault tolerance and limits. Basic support shows the security and limit checks.
glossary.support plan: The AWS support tier an account pays for: Basic (free), Developer, Business, Enterprise. It sets response times and which tools are unlocked.
glossary.CloudTrail: AWS’s audit log: every console click and API call, who made it and when. Event history keeps 90 days free.
glossary.Entra ID: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) — the identity service behind every Azure sign-in: users, groups, MFA, and the roles RBAC assigns.
glossary.security group (Entra): A group of users in Entra ID. Assign a role to the group once, and every member gets it.
glossary.user group: A group of IAM users in AWS. Attach a policy to the group once, and every member gets it.
glossary.MFA: Multi-factor authentication — a second proof at sign-in (an app code, a key), so a stolen password alone is not enough.
glossary.ADR: Architecture Decision Record — one page that says what was decided, what was rejected, and why, so the next team does not reopen it.
